title: Noun + preposition (reason for, cause of etc.)
subtitle: reason for / cause of / increase in
summary: Learn which preposition follows common nouns: a reason for, a cause of, an increase in, a solution to, a connection with.

lesson.heading: noun + for
lesson.text: We say **a demand for ...**, **a need for ...**, **an excuse for ...** and **a reason for ...**.

examples.text: The company went out of business. There was no **demand for** its product any more.
There's no **excuse for** behaviour like that. There's no **need for** it.
The train was late, but nobody knew the **reason for** the delay.

lesson.heading: noun + of
lesson.text: We say **a cause of ...**, **a picture / a photo / a map / a plan / a drawing of ...**, and **an advantage / a disadvantage of ...**.

examples.text: The **cause of** the explosion is unknown.
Rachel showed me some **pictures of** her family.
I had a **map of** the town, so I was able to find my way around.
The **advantage of** living alone is that you can do what you like.

lesson.note: But we say there is an advantage **in** doing something or **to** doing something: There are many advantages **in** living alone. or ... many advantages **to** living alone.

lesson.heading: noun + in
lesson.text: We say **an increase / a decrease / a rise / a fall in** prices, numbers, sales and so on.

examples.text: There has been an **increase in** the number of road accidents recently.
Last year was a bad one for the company. There was a big **fall in** sales.

lesson.heading: noun + to
lesson.text: We say **damage to ...**, **an invitation to ...**, and **a solution to** a problem, **a key to** a door, **an answer to** a question, **a reply to** a letter, **a reaction to** something.

examples.text: The accident was my fault, so I had to pay for the **damage to** the other car.
Did you get an **invitation to** the wedding?
I hope we find a **solution to** the problem.
I was surprised at her **reaction to** my suggestion.
His **attitude to** his job is very negative.
examples.note: or his attitude towards his job

lesson.heading: noun + with / between
lesson.text: We say **a relationship / a connection / contact with** somebody, but **a relationship / a connection / contact / a difference between** two things or people.

examples.text: Do you have a good **relationship with** your parents?
The police want to question a man in **connection with** the robbery.
The police believe that there is no **connection between** the two crimes.
There are some **differences between** British and American English.

lesson.text: Careful: we ask for the cause **of** a problem but look for a solution **to** it.

exercises.prompt: The train was late, but nobody knew the reason ___ the delay.
exercises.explanation: It is always a reason for something, never a reason of.

exercises.prompt: We're trying to solve the problem. We're trying to find a solution ___.
exercises.explanation: A solution to a problem, like an answer to a question.

exercises.prompt: Sue gets on well with her brother. Sue has a good relationship ___ her brother.
exercises.explanation: A relationship with one person; a relationship between two people.

exercises.prompt: The cost of living has gone up a lot. There has been a big increase ___.
exercises.explanation: An increase, a rise, a decrease or a fall in something.

exercises.prompt: Match the two halves of the sentences.

pairs.left: I can't open this door. Do you have a key
The two companies are separate. There is no connection
It wasn't a bad accident. The damage

exercises.prompt: Money isn't the solution ___ every problem.
exercises.explanation: We always say a solution to a problem.

exercises.prompt: The advantage ___ having a car is that you don't have to rely on public transport.
exercises.explanation: The advantage of doing something (but there are advantages in/to doing something).

exercises.statement: I don't know how to answer your question. I can't think of an answer of your question.
exercises.explanation: I can't think of an answer to your question. An answer goes with to.

exercises.prompt: Nobody wants shoes like these any more. There is no demand ___ shoes like these.
exercises.explanation: A demand for something, like a need for something.

exercises.prompt: There are some differences ___ British and American English.
exercises.explanation: A difference between two things or people.

exercises.prompt: James did a very good drawing ___ his father. It looks just like him.
exercises.explanation: A drawing, a picture, a photo or a map of something.
